p.title: Heuristic centrality methods challenge greedy optimization in influence maximization

ext.title: Heuristic centrality methods challenge greedy optimization in influence maximization
ext.document_type: Journal article: empirical comparative study of eight influence maximization algorithms on simulated Independent Cascade diffusion over Facebook subgraphs (open access, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0)
ext.coverage: Read the full text file (1352 lines, about 91k characters, pages 1-18 including references and declarations) in four 250-line chunks plus a final chunk; no section skipped. Metadata hint checked against the text: title, authors, venue, DOI and year all match, so no correction was needed. paul_markup is empty because the task listed no markup files; no sidecar or annotation files were searched for or read. The text is a PDF extraction, so page numbers are inferred from running footers (page 1 = lines 1-46; page 8 = lines 455-551; page 15 = lines 1081-1148).
ext.research_question: Do the theoretical guarantees of influence maximization algorithms (greedy CELF++, sampling-based RIS and IMM) hold in practice, and how do they compare with simple centrality heuristics (Degree, PageRank, Betweenness, Dangling, GCCDC) on spread quality, runtime and scaling under the Independent Cascade model on real social network subgraphs?
ext.theory: Influence maximization is NP-hard under IC and LT (Kempe et al. 2003, ref 12). The influence function is submodular, so greedy selection gives a (1-1/e) approximation (Nemhauser et al. 1978, ref 15). CELF and CELF++ use lazy evaluation to speed up greedy without changing that guarantee. RIS and IMM recast the problem as coverage of reverse-reachable sets with sampling bounds. Centrality heuristics carry no guarantee and are justified as cheap structural proxies. The paper's framing: asymptotic guarantees can diverge from practice because hidden constants, network structure and implementation matter (p.4, lines 260-269; p.13, lines 948-961).
ext.data: Source: Facebook ego network from the SNAP collection, 4,039 nodes and 88,234 undirected edges (p.6, lines 402-404). Sampled subgraphs: 200, 500, 800 and 1000 nodes per Methods and Table 2 (p.6, p.8); the abstract instead says 200, 400, 600, 800 and 1,000 nodes (p.1). Unit: one seed set per algorithm, size and run. Count: 8 algorithms x 4 sizes x 10 independent runs (seeds 42-51) = 320 seed sets, each scored by 50 Monte Carlo IC simulations (p.6, lines 411-434). No time period; a static snapshot of the 2014 SNAP dataset.
ext.method: Eight algorithms, implemented in Python 3.8 with NumPy 1.21 and NetworkX 2.6 (p.8): CELF++ (50 MC per marginal-gain estimate); RIS with theta = min(10000, 50n); IMM with epsilon = 0.2; Degree; PageRank (damping 0.85, power iteration, tolerance 1e-6, max 100 iterations); Betweenness (Brandes); Dangling centrality; GCCDC (p.4-6). Diffusion: IC with uniform p = 0.1 on all edges; seed budget k = 10. Subgraphs drawn by importance sampling: node importance is the average of normalised degree centrality and normalised PageRank; top-ranked nodes plus their highest-importance neighbours are kept to keep the subgraph connected (p.6, lines 402-410). Evaluation: mean spread over 50 MC simulations per seed set; 10 runs per configuration; mean, SD, min, max and CV reported; wall-clock seconds; spread per second as efficiency (p.7-8). Significance: paired t-tests with Bonferroni correction (alpha 0.05), with Mann-Whitney U said to give the same results (p.7-8, p.8).
ext.identification: None in a causal sense. This is a controlled simulation benchmark: algorithms are compared on identical subgraphs under the same IC settings, and seeds are paired across runs for the t-tests. No natural experiment or instrument is used.
ext.scope: One real-world network (Facebook ego network subgraphs) at 200-1000 nodes; one diffusion model (IC, uniform p = 0.1); one seed budget (k = 10); undirected graphs only. Not tested: directed, weighted or temporal networks; other diffusion models; large-scale graphs; deep RL or GNN methods. The paper says the sampled subgraphs have degree exponent above 3 (p.6, lines 408-409).

key_findings.finding: CELF++ performs far below the other algorithms at 1000 nodes (about 12.9% of IMM), despite its (1-1/e) guarantee. The authors attribute this mainly to only 50 MC simulations per estimate and Python implementation, not to an algorithmic flaw.
key_findings.location: Results p.8 (lines 473-486); Discussion p.13 (lines 948-955); Conclusion p.15-16
key_findings.numbers: CELF++ 122.95 +/- 24.37 vs IMM 954.90 +/- 1.27; ratio 12.9%; Delta 831.95, t = -107.78, p < 0.001. Abstract (p.1) says 11.2%, which conflicts.

key_findings.finding: IMM is best at 1000 nodes and RIS is close behind. The IMM-RIS gap is small but significant.
PageRank and Betweenness are statistically indistinguishable and reach about 96.5% of IMM spread at 1000 nodes, at 0.4 s and 8.8 s respectively.
key_findings.location: Results p.8-9 (lines 474-476, 495-499); Table 3 p.11; efficiency p.10 (lines 658-666); Discussion p.13 and p.15
key_findings.numbers: PageRank 921.78 +/- 3.28; Betweenness 921.80 +/- 3.34; Delta -0.02, t = -0.01, p = 0.99; PageRank vs IMM Delta 33.12, t = 26.97, p < 0.001. The paper states 96.3% in the abstract, Discussion and Conclusion, but 921.78/954.90 = 96.5%. Stated 794x runtime speed-up: 323.5/0.4 = 809x from the paper's own times.

key_findings.finding: Degree, GCCDC and Dangling form a lower cluster around 80-85% of IMM spread. Dangling is lowest. GCCDC does not improve on Degree at 1000 nodes.
key_findings.location: Results p.8 (lines 475-477); Algorithm-specific observations p.12 (lines 893-908); Broader Discussion p.15 (lines 1123-1129)
key_findings.numbers: Degree 810.87 +/- 6.77; GCCDC 811.59 +/- 5.00; Dangling 797.44 +/- 12.05 (CV up to 6.24%). Degree vs Dangling t = 2.67, p < 0.05; GCCDC vs Dangling t = 2.90, p < 0.05.

key_findings.finding: Sampling methods (IMM, RIS) have very low variance and scale near-linearly. Heuristics have moderate CVs. CELF++ is unstable, with a non-monotone trajectory.
key_findings.location: Scalability p.9 (lines 558-576); Algorithm-specific observations p.11-12 (lines 868-875); Fig. 4 p.10
key_findings.numbers: IMM CV 0.07-0.17%; RIS CV 0.13-0.23%; Betweenness CV 0.16-0.36%; PageRank 0.14-0.25%; Degree 0.66-2.59%; CELF++ CV rose to 71.5% at 500 nodes (p.10, line 646).

key_findings.finding: Growth from 200 to 1000 nodes is close to proportional for most methods. The text and Table 4 disagree for some entries.
key_findings.numbers: Text: IMM +402%, RIS +399%, PageRank +403%, Degree +411%, CELF++ +633%. Table 4: IMM +402%, RIS +400%, PageRank +404%, Degree +410%, CELF++ +740%. CELF++ at 500 nodes is 4.56 in the text and 4.91 in Table 2.

key_findings.finding: Efficiency ranking: PageRank 2,304 spread/s; Degree 2,027; Dangling 1,994; GCCDC 279.86; Betweenness 104.75; RIS 14.68; IMM 2.95; CELF++ 0.18 (all at 1000 nodes).
key_findings.location: Computational efficiency p.10 (lines 658-664); Fig. 3 caption p.9
key_findings.numbers: PageRank 921.78 spread / 0.4 s; IMM 954.90 / 323.5 s; CELF++ 122.95 / 688.4 s max runtime. RIS vs PageRank: 3.3% lower spread for 162x runtime (p.10-11).

key_findings.finding: Extrapolated runtimes to 10,000 nodes are reported but were not measured.
key_findings.numbers: RIS about 795 s; IMM about 3970 s; CELF++ about 840 s at 1000 nodes and over 8,400 s at 10,000 nodes (linear extrapolation). The limitations section also quotes PageRank at about 5 s at 10,000 nodes, a figure not given in the Discussion. Linear scaling from RIS's 64.9 s would give about 649 s, not 795 s.

measures: Mean influence spread over 50 IC Monte Carlo simulations per seed set
Across 10 runs: mean, SD, min, max, coefficient of variation
Wall-clock runtime in seconds, from algorithm start to seed-set output
Scaling growth percentage relative to the 200-node baseline
Paired t-test and Mann-Whitney U, Bonferroni-corrected, for pairwise differences at 1000 nodes
Centrality measures: degree, PageRank (alpha 0.85), betweenness (Brandes), dangling centrality (degree as proxy for connectivity), GCCDC
limitations: Stated by the authors (p.14, lines 1017-1098): only one real-world network (Facebook), so results may not transfer to directed, weighted or temporal networks.
Stated: uniform IC probability p = 0.1 only, with no weighted-cascade or LT model; the authors expect ranking changes under other models.
Stated: a single seed budget (k = 10); behaviour at k = 1-3 or k > 50 is not tested.
Stated: scales limited to 200-1000 nodes; results at millions to billions of nodes are extrapolated and not validated.

Stated: CELF++ used only 50 MC simulations per estimate versus 10,000+ in practice, using a Python 3.8 implementation; the authors say the underperformance is likely a budget and implementation artefact, not a flaw in the algorithm.

Stated: importance-based sampling (top degree and PageRank nodes) may densify the subgraph around hubs and favour centrality heuristics; the authors claim robustness to the extraction method without testing it.
Stated: no comparison with deep RL or GNN methods (PIANO and others); the authors say such a comparison is future work.

Reader-noted, not stated by the authors: (a) abstract subgraph sizes (200, 400, 600, 800, 1000) differ from Methods and Table 2 (200, 500, 800, 1000); (b) abstract gives CELF++ as 11.2% of sampling-based spread, but the body gives 12.9%; (c) PageRank is given as 96.3% of IMM, but Table 2 gives 96.5%; (d) the 794x runtime ratio does not match 323.5/0.4 = 809x; (e) RIS uses theta = min(10000, 50n), which equals 10,000 at every tested size, so it is a fixed budget rather than theory-determined; (f) the Dangling centrality implementation uses degree as a proxy for connectivity impact (p.6, lines 389-390), so the method tested is not the published metric; (g) Mann-Whitney results are described only qualitatively, and Bonferroni-adjusted p-values are not reported; (h) p.15 line 1117 refers to heuristics 'we proposed in SATIC', an undefined term, and the Broader implications paragraph (lines 1100-1101) contains an unclear sentence about CELF guarantees for static allocations; (i) refs 9-11 (traffic anomaly detection, side-channel attacks, sample-size guidance) are cited for influence-maximization claims but are off-topic; ref 52 lacks authors and ref 54 lists 'Others'; (j) abstract IMM 955.24 and RIS 951.27 do not match Table 2 at 1000 nodes (954.90 and 952.53) and are not explained.

short_quotes.quote: The findings indicate a significant disparity between theoretical guarantees and actual performance
short_quotes.location: Abstract, p.1 (lines 12-13). Only one quote is given, per the copyright limit on reproducing observed text.

rel.summary_md:
Almazaydeh et al. compare eight influence-maximization methods under the Independent Cascade (IC) model. The graphs are Facebook ego-network subgraphs of 200 to 1,000 nodes, with uniform p = 0.1, k = 10 seeds, 10 runs and 50 Monte Carlo (MC) simulations per seed set. At 1,000 nodes, IMM is best (954.90) and RIS is close behind (952.53, five times faster). PageRank and Betweenness cannot be told apart (about 921.8, or 96.5% of IMM; the paper itself says 96.3%), and PageRank runs in 0.4 s. Degree, GCCDC and Dangling reach about 80-85% of IMM. CELF++ collapses to 12.9% of IMM (the abstract says 11.2%), with a CV of up to 71.5%. The authors blame only 50 MC simulations per marginal estimate plus a Python implementation, but they never test that explanation. The study has several internal inconsistencies: subgraph sizes, percentages, the 794x speed-up and the extrapolated runtimes do not match the paper's own tables.

This paper is already wired into Melange. `fec/engine/mc_stability_check.py` names it as its motivation. The skill library cites it to argue that the frontier's MC=20 greedy is safe because common random numbers (CRN) mean every candidate is compared under the same draws. That reasoning is sound for comparing marginals. The problem is that the recorded pass is older than a 2026-10-01 fix. The pass (MEA-7, holistic graph: 100% at MC=100, 98% across RNG seeds) was measured before QME fix 3. Before that fix, the splitmix keys did not depend on SEED, so the 'different RNG seed' runs reused the same edge and seed-activation draws. The MC=100 leg still holds, though it shares its first 20 iterations with production. The cross-seed leg did not test independent draws.

The paper's other point, that cheap centrality gets within a few percent of IMM, suggests a cheap ablation the system lacks: run a PageRank, degree or Katz-Bonacich seed baseline through the same CRN cascade. It would be an ablation only, because stance gating and seed activation are things centrality cannot see. The joint optimizer is untouched by this paper. It is deterministic (no MC), so the CELF++ failure mode cannot occur there.

bearings.paper_claim: Lazy greedy (CELF++) with too few MC simulations per marginal estimate (50) is unstable and badly suboptimal: at 1,000 nodes it reaches 12.9% of IMM (122.95 +/- 24.37 vs 954.90 +/- 1.27; t = -107.78), and its CV peaks at 71.5% at 500 nodes. The authors blame the MC budget and the implementation, but they do not test this.
bearings.paper_location: Results p.8 (lines 473-486); p.10 (line 646); Discussion p.13 (lines 948-955); Limitations p.14
bearings.system_side: The frontier runs lazy greedy up to 60 seeds at MC=20 (fewer simulations than the paper's 50). It is protected by edge-keyed CRN: each (iteration, edge) draw comes from splitmix, so spread(S+c) and spread(S) share their draws. mc_stability_check.py was written in response to this paper. It compares production against MC=100 and against SEED=1 and SEED=13. Brain MEA-7 records a PASS on the holistic graph (100% Jaccard at MC=100, 98% across seeds). However, QME fix 3 (2026-10-01) says that before it, 'SEED!=7 reruns reused identical draws and understated seed variance', because the _SO key offset did not exist. The cross-seed leg of MEA-7, and the CU-vintage 100% record cited at salience_shock.py:44, were therefore measured when only the bystander random.random() stream changed between seeds.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's failure mode is independently noisy marginal estimates, and CRN removes it for pairwise comparisons. That part carries over as support for the CRN design, not as a threat. What does not carry over is the old evidence that the selected seed set is stable across independent realizations. That evidence must be re-measured under the post-fix keying. The MC=100 leg stays valid (iterations 0-99 include 80 new draws). This is a new agent analysis, so it is UNVERIFIED (DE-062), and re-running the engine is Paul's call. The paper's graphs are undirected with uniform p, while Melange uses competitive IC with seed gating on a 533-node directed or symmetrized kernel. The paper's numbers are evidence of the mechanism only.

bearings.paper_claim: At 1,000 nodes, PageRank seeds reach 921.78 / 954.90 = 96.5% of IMM spread in 0.4 s (IMM takes 323.5 s). Betweenness matches PageRank (t = -0.01, p = 0.99). Degree reaches about 85%.
bearings.paper_location: Results p.8-9 (lines 474-476, 495-499); Table 2-3 p.8, p.11; efficiency p.10 (lines 658-666)
bearings.system_side: Before greedy runs, the frontier and the coalition allocator cut the candidate pool to the top 45 neutral members by engagement x priority x delivery_mult. That cut is a heuristic too, and it has never been compared with anything. No run measures what greedy adds over a cheap structural seed rule (degree, PageRank or Katz-Bonacich on the same kernel) scored by the same CRN cascade.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This is useful only as an ablation diagnostic, run the way kb_benchmark is run (read-only, consumed by nothing). The paper's hub-favoring subgraph sampling (degree plus PageRank importance) tilts results toward centrality heuristics. Melange's objective adds stance-gated pools, seed_prob x SGATE activation and rival-industry bystanders, none of which centrality can see. So a near-match on spread would not justify replacing greedy. A large gap would quantify what stance-aware selection buys. Spread here is modeled cascade reach, not evidence of real access or influence (D-025).

bearings.paper_claim: Theoretical guarantees such as greedy's (1-1/e) bound can diverge sharply from realized performance when marginal gains are estimated by noisy simulation. CELF++ reached only 12.9% of IMM.
bearings.system_side: The joint optimizer runs CELF lazy greedy over the deterministic closed-form pflip winnability, with no Monte Carlo. Within a fixed stance state, it numerically checks that the objective is separable by member and concave. It then claims an exact optimum on the $500 grid and reports the (1-1/e) floor and the Golovin-Krause bound only as context. When a modeled conversion happens, it voids the certificate instead of claiming a guarantee.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's gap between guarantee and practice comes from MC estimation error and does not transfer to a deterministic objective. Its evidence therefore does not undercut the optimizer's guarantee, which already rests on a verified fixed-state concavity certificate, not on submodular-greedy theory. The paper is relevant only if the optimizer's objective is ever replaced by a simulated cascade.

bearings.paper_claim: Simple centrality rankings used as seed rules come close to sampling-based IM under IC (PageRank 96.5% of IMM), at a tiny fraction of the runtime (2,304 spread/s vs 2.95 for IMM).
bearings.system_side: kb_benchmark computes Katz-Bonacich centrality on the live kernel P = build_P(adj). It reports only Spearman correlations against the allocation, observed money and the legislative score (MEA-6 holistic: KB vs allocation +0.225). It never scores KB-top-k as a seed set under the cascade.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Adding one more column to kb_benchmark (the spread of KB-top-k seeds under the frontier's CRN cascade) would answer, on Melange's own kernel, the question the paper answers on Facebook. It must stay a diagnostic labeled UNSTRATIFIED, with its window, denominator (533 members) and topic named. The KB score remains a model output, not a measure of access.

bearings.paper_claim: PageRank and betweenness are near-interchangeable proxies for IC spread on undirected graphs (921.78 vs 921.80, p = 0.99). The paper tests no directed or weighted networks.
bearings.system_side: InfluenceScore (0.60 out-degree + 0.25 betweenness + 0.15 eigenvector) was retired from the Influence pillar on 2026-06-25 (AB13 = 0) because it is blind to direction. It still feeds the underdog lens.
bearings.code_ref: congress_centrality_*.xlsx; Blended Model AB12/AB13 (workbook; no Python line)
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper shows centrality predicts simulated cascade spread, not legislative effect or bill passage. It covers undirected graphs only, so it does not address the reason the score was retired. The paper gives no grounds to reinstate it.

gaps_exposed: The cross-seed leg of the MC-stability check was not re-measured after QME fix 3 (2026-10-01) added SEED-dependent splitmix keys. The recorded '98% across RNG seeds' (MEA-7) and the CU-vintage '100% overlap' therefore did not test independent edge and seed-activation draws.
No heuristic seed baseline (degree, PageRank or Katz-Bonacich on build_P) has been scored under the same CRN cascade. What greedy selection adds over cheap structural seeding is unmeasured.
The top-45 candidate pre-cut (engagement x priority x delivery) is itself a heuristic that has never been compared with an alternative pre-cut or with no pre-cut.
Neither the frontier nor the coalition output reports spread variance (SD or CV) across RNG seeds. The paper treats run-to-run CV as a first-class quality measure.
flags: The system's citations misquote the paper. mc_stability_check.py:4-5 and .claude/skills/influence-modeling-reference/SKILL.md:108 give '11.2%' (the abstract figure; the body and Table 2 give 12.9%). They call it '11.2% of true spread', but it is a share of IMM spread. The skill also says the paper 'showed' that noisy MC estimates corrupt lazy greedy. The paper only offers the MC budget and implementation as a likely cause, untested. These are skill and docstring wording fixes for Paul to approve; nothing was edited.

STALE VALIDATION: .claude/skills/moneyball-config-and-flags/SKILL.md:102, moneyball-architecture-contract/SKILL.md:107, salience_shock.py:44 and brain STATE.md:765 all treat MC=20 as validated across RNG seeds. That evidence predates the SEED-keying fix in budget_frontier.py:66-69, so the cross-seed agreement was partly by construction. This agent analysis is UNVERIFIED (DE-062) until a second path reproduces it, and re-running mc_stability_check is Paul's call under the quant-model-evaluation melange binding (line 22).

D-025: the paper's centrality results concern simulated IC reach. They must not be used to describe layer-balanced staffer PageRank, or any graph rank, as closeness, access or introduction likelihood.
The paper argues for neither rejected SNA proposal (dropping regular cosponsorship edges, per-edge volume normalization). There is no conflict there.

The paper has internal numeric inconsistencies (subgraph sizes 200/400/600/800/1000 vs 200/500/800/1000; 96.3% vs 96.5%; 794x vs 809x; abstract IMM 955.24 and RIS 951.27 vs Table 2 at 954.90 and 952.53; RIS theta fixed at 10,000 at every size). Quote only the Table 2 numbers.
rel.paul_alignment: Paul has no annotation on this paper. His joint-optimizer position treats adaptive greedy plus CELF as the operational layer, with GCOMB-style learned policies taking over at scale. The paper does not threaten that position for optimize.py, which is deterministic. For MC-driven greedy (frontier, coalition), the paper supports it only when marginal estimates are reliable. At 533 nodes, scale is not the binding constraint, so the paper gives no reason to move to RIS, IMM or a learned policy; the brain note 'RIS/IMM unneeded at 533 nodes' agrees. On centrality, Paul says more research on forms of centrality is needed, and the paper adds that PageRank and betweenness are equivalent as spread proxies. That evidence comes only from undirected graphs with uniform p, so it does not touch his interest in directionality (Haythornthwaite) or the retirement of direction-blind centrality. The system-side record is what is stale: the cross-seed MC stability claim predates the 2026-10-01 SEED-keying fix.

related.why: This is the source of the data-dependent bound the joint optimizer reports. The Almazaydeh paper shows that such guarantees break down in practice when marginals are estimated by noisy simulation.
It grounds the seed-activation gate inside the frontier's cascade. That gate is the stance and receptivity factor that centrality heuristics like those benchmarked here cannot see.
Another influence-maximization benchmark on IC, using graph embeddings and GNNs. Almazaydeh lists learned methods as untested future work.
A survey of behavior-aware IM. It covers the receiver-susceptibility and seed-probability extensions that the uniform-p setup here leaves out.
Efficient IM under the IC model. It addresses the same runtime-versus-quality trade-off this paper measures.
Melange's frontier runs competitive two-color IC (Bharathi-Kempe-Salek), a setting this single-color benchmark does not test.
Katz-Bonacich centrality as the equilibrium allocation rule. This paper's evidence that centrality heuristics work well suggests scoring KB seed sets under the cascade.

Sotoudeh finds eigenvector centrality is a weak indicator of bill passage, whereas this paper finds centrality a strong proxy for simulated spread. Together they show that spread proxies are not legislative influence.
Background on Monte Carlo sample size. The paper's CELF++ failure is a case of an inadequate MC budget.
Learned IM policies are the alternative this paper defers. Paul's GCOMB-style learned-policy expectation sits in this lineage.
